record.paper_title: Bootstrap Algebraic Multigrid: status report, open problems, and outlook
record.original_question: For general Hermitian positive definite problems, how can the compatible-relaxation, algebraic-distance, least-squares-interpolation, and bootstrap test-vector components of bootstrap algebraic multigrid be integrated into an overall algorithm that is practical, easy to tune, and robust as a fast multigrid solver across a diverse set of test problems, including systems of partial differential equations?

evidence.quote: The main issue to consider in developing BAMG as a fast solver for general HPD problems concerns the integration of the BAMG components in order to obtain an overall algorithm for use in practice.
Specifically, a systematic study of the BAMG processes for a carefully chosen and diverse set of test problems (that includes systems of PDEs) is needed.
An integration of all BAMG components to obtain an easy to tune and robust multigrid solver.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider Hermitian positive definite (HPD) linear systems Ax = b arising from discretizations of partial differential equations, including systems of PDEs. Bootstrap Algebraic Multigrid (BAMG) is a multilevel iterative methodology composed of the following principal components:

1. Compatible Relaxation (CR): a relaxation scheme on the fine-degrees-of-freedom subset used to identify a coarse variable set C ⊂ Ω such that the CR convergence rate ρ_CR is small, providing an a posteriori measure of the suitability of the coarse set.
2. Algebraic Distance: a measure d(i,j) between degrees of freedom derived from a small set of smoothed test vectors (typically obtained by relaxing on the homogeneous system Ax = 0 from random initial guesses) that is used to form interpolation sparsity patterns / caliber.
3. Least-Squares Interpolation: given a coarse set C and a set of test vectors {v_k}_{k=1}^K, the interpolation operator P is defined row-wise by minimizing, for each fine point i, the weighted least-squares functional Σ_k ω_k (v_k(i) − Σ_{j∈C_i} P_{ij} v_k(j))^2 over admissible sparsity patterns C_i.
4. Bootstrap Test-Vector Setup: a self-correcting cycle in which a multigrid hierarchy built from current test vectors is itself applied (as a generalized eigensolver / smoother) on the homogeneous problem to produce improved test vectors, which are then fed back to redefine the coarse sets, algebraic distances, and least-squares interpolations.

Problem. Devise an explicit algorithmic specification that integrates all four components above into a single BAMG setup-and-solve algorithm for general HPD problems with the following properties:

(a) Practicality: setup and per-cycle costs are bounded by a modest constant times the cost of a sparse matrix–vector product with A, with provably bounded operator complexity and grid complexity.
(b) Ease of tuning: the algorithm exposes only a small, fixed number of user parameters (e.g., number of test vectors K, number of bootstrap cycles, CR tolerance, interpolation caliber), with default values that perform well across problem classes without per-problem hand tuning.
(c) Robustness: the resulting V-cycle (or W-cycle) yields a uniformly bounded asymptotic convergence factor ρ < 1 independent of problem size and of standard parameters (e.g., mesh size, anisotropy, jumps in coefficients) over a diverse benchmark suite that includes scalar elliptic PDEs with variable/jumping coefficients, anisotropic diffusion, and HPD systems of PDEs (e.g., linear elasticity, Stokes-type HPD reformulations, Maxwell-type HPD problems).

Specify the algorithm, prove (or provide strong empirical evidence supported by analysis) that properties (a)–(c) hold, and demonstrate uniform convergence on a representative diverse test set of HPD problems including PDE systems.
artifact.status_search_result: The question is posed as an open research direction in the BAMG literature: integrating compatible relaxation, algebraic distance, least-squares interpolation, and bootstrap test-vector setup into a single robust, easy-to-tune solver for general HPD problems including PDE systems. Subsequent works (Brandt–Brannick–Kahl–Livshits and follow-ups, including BAMG for nonsymmetric and Markov chain problems) have advanced individual components and partial integrations, but no published result establishes a fully integrated, parameter-light, provably robust BAMG solver across a broad HPD benchmark including PDE systems. The problem appears to remain open.
